title: Biology — Complete Secondary & Foundation Course
short_description: A complete biology course from the characteristics of life to genetics, ecology, human and plant biology — with practicals, quizzes and a final examination.
description: This is a complete, classroom-ready biology course for secondary, senior secondary and foundation-level students. It covers the full scheme of work: foundations of biology, cell biology, biological molecules, cell division, genetics, evolution, ecology, human biology, plant biology and practical biology, followed by structured revision and a final examination. Every lesson contains original WOLI DAN TECH HUB teaching material — theory, worked examples, key concepts and summaries — plus verified videos and open textbooks. Each module includes a hands-on practical activity, a written assignment, a quiz and a module examination. To complete the course and earn a certificate, students must finish at least 80% of lessons, keep a quiz average of 60% or above, pass every assignment and pass the final examination.
prerequisites: No previous biology required — Module 1 starts from zero
target_audience: Junior and senior secondary school students
Students preparing for WAEC, NECO and JAMB biology
Adult learners starting a science pathway
learning_objectives: Describe the characteristics of living things and levels of biological organisation
Explain cell structure, transport processes and cell division
Classify biological molecules and explain enzyme action
Solve Mendelian genetics problems including monohybrid crosses
Explain natural selection and the evidence for evolution
Analyse ecosystems, food chains, nutrient cycles and human impact
Describe the major human body systems and how they stay balanced
Explain photosynthesis, transport and reproduction in flowering plants
Carry out safe biology practicals including microscopy and food tests
Interpret biological data, graphs and examination questions accurately
learning_outcomes: Define and apply the seven characteristics of living organisms
Label plant and animal cells and state the function of each organelle
Test foods for starch, sugar, protein and fats and explain each test
Describe mitosis and meiosis and compare their outcomes
Use Punnett squares to predict genotypes and phenotypes
Explain how natural selection produces adaptation over generations
Construct food chains and pyramids and explain energy loss
Trace digestion, circulation and gaseous exchange in humans
Write the photosynthesis equation and explain limiting factors
Use a light microscope safely and calculate total magnification
Plan, record and evaluate a simple biological investigation
Score at least 60% in the final biology examination
skills_gained: Data handling: tables, graphs and magnification calculations
Genetic problem solving with Punnett squares
requirements: A notebook or device for study notes
Pen, pencil and ruler for biological drawings
Access to the internet for videos and quizzes (low-bandwidth friendly)
For practicals: household-safe materials listed in each activity (no dangerous chemicals)
instructor_name: WOLI DAN TECH HUB Science Faculty

final_exam.title: Biology — Final Examination
final_exam.description: The final examination for the complete biology course. It tests every module: foundations, cells, molecules, division, genetics, evolution, ecology, human biology, plant biology and practical skills.
final_exam.instructions: Answer ALL 30 questions. Each question carries equal marks. You have 90 minutes and a maximum of 3 attempts — your best attempt counts. The pass mark is 60%. Read each question carefully, eliminate wrong options first, and check flagged questions before submitting. Calculators are NOT required; magnification and percentage questions use simple numbers.

questions.question: A student observes that yeast produces bubbles in warm sugar water, but the same mixture with boiled yeast produces nothing. Which characteristic of living things does this BEST demonstrate?
questions.explanation: Live yeast respires anaerobically, fermenting sugar and releasing carbon dioxide (the bubbles). Boiled (dead) yeast cannot respire, so nothing happens — showing that metabolism is a property of living cells.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the correct order of biological organisation from simplest to most complex?
questions.explanation: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into systems, and systems make up the organism.

questions.question: A student uses a microscope with a x10 eyepiece and a x40 objective lens. The total magnification is:
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = x400.

questions.question: Which organelle is correctly matched with its function?
options: Chloroplast — controlling what enters the cell
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing energy (ATP) from glucose. Packaging is the Golgi body, entry control is the cell membrane, and the nucleus stores genetic instructions.

questions.question: True or False: Bacterial cells are prokaryotic because they lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
questions.explanation: True. Prokaryotic cells (bacteria) have DNA free in the cytoplasm and no membrane-bound organelles, unlike eukaryotic plant and animal cells.

questions.question: A food sample stays brown with iodine solution but gives a purple colour with biuret solution. The sample contains:
questions.explanation: Iodine stays brown-yellow when starch is absent, and biuret turns purple in the presence of protein. So the sample has protein but no starch.

questions.question: Why does a high temperature (e.g. 80°C) permanently stop most human enzymes from working?
options: The enzyme is denatured — its active site loses shape
questions.explanation: Excess heat breaks the weak bonds holding the enzyme's shape, so the active site no longer fits the substrate. This denaturation is usually irreversible.

questions.question: Which row correctly links each food to its main nutrient and test result?
options: Bread + iodine → blue-black; egg white + biuret → purple
Bread + biuret → purple; oil + iodine → blue-black
Glucose + iodine → blue-black; starch + Benedict's (heated) → brick red
Egg white + iodine → blue-black; bread + biuret → purple
questions.explanation: Bread is rich in starch (iodine → blue-black) and egg white is protein (biuret → purple). Benedict's tests reducing sugars, not starch.

questions.question: During which phase of mitosis do chromosomes line up along the cell equator?
questions.explanation: In metaphase, spindle fibres pull chromosomes into a single line at the equator before sister chromatids separate in anaphase.

questions.question: A human body cell (46 chromosomes) divides by meiosis. Each gamete produced will contain:
options: 46 chromosomes, genetically identical to the parent
23 chromosomes, genetically different due to crossing over and independent assortment
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number (46 → 23) and crossing over plus independent assortment make each gamete genetically unique.

questions.question: True or False: Mitosis produces two genetically identical diploid cells and is used for growth and repair, while meiosis produces gametes.
questions.explanation: True. Mitosis conserves chromosome number for growth/repair; meiosis halves it to form gametes for sexual reproduction.

questions.question: In pea plants, tall (T) is dominant over short (t). A cross between two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt) is expected to produce short offspring with probability:
questions.explanation: The Punnett square gives genotypes TT, Tt, Tt, tt — only tt (1 out of 4) is short.

questions.question: A woman who is a carrier for haemophilia (XHXh) has children with a normal man (XHY). What is the probability that a SON is affected?
questions.explanation: Sons get Y from the father and either XH or Xh from the mother, so half the sons (XhY) are affected. Sex-linked recessive traits show up more in males.

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes genotype from phenotype?
options: Genotype is observable; phenotype is hidden
Genotype is the allele combination; phenotype is the observable trait produced with the environment
Genotype changes daily; phenotype is fixed at birth
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: Genotype (e.g. Tt) is the inherited allele pair; phenotype (e.g. tall) is the expressed trait resulting from genotype plus environment.

questions.question: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria become common in a hospital after years of antibiotic use. The BEST Darwinian explanation is:
options: The antibiotic created resistant mutants on purpose
Resistant variants already present survived and reproduced while others died — natural selection
Bacteria learned to eat the antibiotic
All bacteria merged into one resistant super-cell
questions.explanation: Variation already exists; the antibiotic is a selection pressure. Resistant cells survive and pass on their alleles, so resistance spreads — natural selection in action.

questions.question: Which of the following are lines of evidence for evolution? (Select ALL that apply)
options: Fossils showing gradual change over rock layers
Homologous structures (e.g. pentadactyl limbs) with common ancestry
Identical DNA in every species on Earth
Observed natural selection such as pesticide resistance
questions.explanation: Fossils, homologies (anatomical, developmental, molecular) and directly observed selection all support evolution. DNA is similar between related species but never identical across all species.

questions.question: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. If a pesticide accumulates at each feeding level, which organism will have the HIGHEST concentration?
questions.explanation: Biomagnification: persistent toxins concentrate up the food chain, so the top predator (hawk) carries the highest load.

questions.question: Only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is mainly:
options: Lost through respiration, movement, excretion and uneaten parts
questions.explanation: Most energy is used for life processes (respiration), lost as heat, or never eaten — which is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 levels.

questions.question: Which pair of processes keeps atmospheric carbon dioxide cycling between organisms and the air?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis removes CO2 while respiration and combustion return it — the core of the carbon cycle, balanced over time.

questions.question: Bile plays an important role in fat digestion because it:
options: Contains enzymes that digest fat to glycerol
Emulsifies fats into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for lipase
Absorbs fatty acids into the blood directly
questions.explanation: Bile has no enzymes; it emulsifies fat (physical digestion) and neutralises stomach acid, giving lipase huge surface area to work on.

questions.question: Why is the left ventricle wall of the heart much thicker than the right ventricle wall?
options: It stores extra blood for emergencies
It must pump blood all the way round the body at high pressure
It receives blood from the lungs
It prevents backflow into the atria
questions.explanation: The left ventricle drives the systemic circulation (whole body), needing far more pressure than the right ventricle's short trip to the lungs.

questions.question: Which adaptations make alveoli efficient at gas exchange? (best single answer)
options: Large total surface area, thin one-cell walls, moist lining and dense capillaries
A waterproof coating that blocks germs
questions.explanation: Millions of thin-walled, moist alveoli wrapped in capillaries give a huge surface for fast diffusion of O2 in and CO2 out.

questions.question: A potted plant is kept in the dark for 48 hours, then one leaf is covered with foil except a star shape, and the plant is placed in sunlight. After testing the leaf for starch, starch appears ONLY in the star. This proves that:
options: Carbon dioxide is needed for photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Destarching removes prior starch. Only the part of the leaf that received light forms new starch, proving light is necessary for photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which row correctly states the transport tissues and what they carry?
options: Xylem carries sugars down; phloem carries water up
Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries sugars (translocation) both ways
Xylem carries oxygen; phloem carries carbon dioxide
Both xylem and phloem carry only water
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels move water/minerals upward (transpiration pull); phloem sieve tubes translocate sugars from sources to sinks in any direction.

questions.question: An onion cell viewed at x100 appears 40 mm wide in the drawing. The real cell width is approximately:
questions.explanation: Real size = image size ÷ magnification = 40 mm ÷ 100 = 0.4 mm (400 micrometres — a realistic plant cell width).

questions.question: A student heats Benedict's solution with a sample and gets a brick-red precipitate. The correct conclusion and safety note are:
options: Starch present; Benedict's can be tasted to confirm
Protein present; heat with an open flame for speed
A high concentration of reducing sugar is present; wear eye protection and point the tube away when heating
No sugar present; the test failed
questions.explanation: Brick-red with Benedict's (heated) means abundant reducing sugar. Safe practice: goggles on, and never point a heated tube at anyone.

questions.question: A student investigates how light intensity affects photosynthesis using pondweed bubbles per minute. Which features make this a fair, valid experiment? (Select ALL that apply)
options: Only the lamp distance changes; temperature, CO2 and pondweed amount stay constant
Each distance is repeated and a mean is calculated
The student counts bubbles for the same fixed time at each distance
The student uses a different pondweed species at each distance for variety
questions.explanation: Fair test = one independent variable (light), controlled variables, repeats with means, and fixed counting time. Changing species adds an uncontrolled variable.

questions.question: In an osmosis experiment, a yam strip in concentrated salt solution loses mass while one in distilled water gains mass. The BEST explanation is:
options: Salt actively pumps water out of cells
Water moves by osmosis from high to low water concentration across the partially permeable cell membranes
The yam respires faster in salt
Distilled water dissolves the cell walls
questions.explanation: Osmosis moves water down its concentration gradient: out of cells into the salty solution (mass loss), and into cells from distilled water (mass gain, turgor).

questions.question: Sickle-cell anaemia persists in malaria regions because heterozygotes (HbAHbS) resist malaria while homozygotes suffer. This is an example of:
options: Balanced polymorphism maintained by heterozygote advantage
Genetic drift in a small population
A acquired characteristic passed to offspring
questions.explanation: Heterozygote advantage keeps both alleles in the population: carriers survive malaria better than HbAHbA and avoid sickle-cell disease unlike HbSHbS.

questions.question: True or False: In a pyramid of biomass for a typical grassland, the producer level is the widest because producers capture the ecosystem's energy input.
questions.explanation: True. Producers hold the most biomass since all ecosystem energy enters through them; each higher level keeps only ~10%.
